steps.say: Four different measures, one small data set. Start by getting your bearings in the data.

steps.pre: How many street counts are listed?
steps.done: The mean always divides by this count, so get it right first.
steps.hint: Count the numbers in the list one by one.

steps.pre: Add the six counts together. What is the total?
steps.hint: Add them in pairs: 5 + 7, then 8 + 7, then 9 + 6.

steps.pre: Divide the total by the number of streets to get the mean.
steps.done: The mean uses every value, so a single unusual street would move it.
steps.hint: Share the total equally between the six streets.

steps.say: Sorted smallest to largest, the counts run 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9.

steps.pre: With six values there is no single middle one. Add the two middle values and divide by 2. What is the median?
steps.hint: The third and fourth values in the sorted list are the middle pair.

steps.pre: Which count appears more than once? That is the mode.
steps.hint: Tally each value and look for the one that repeats.

steps.pre: Subtract the smallest count from the largest to get the range.
steps.done: Mean, median and mode all landed on the same number here, which tells you the data is evenly spread.

steps.say: Check: the mean and median must both sit inside the range of the data, between 5 and 9. They do, so the answers are believable.

bronze.display: A student counted the cars parked on six streets: 5, 7, 8, 7, 9, 6. Find the mean, median, mode and range.

steps.say: Here each value is repeated many times, so you cannot just add four numbers and divide by four.

steps.pre: How many different daisy counts are listed in the table?
steps.done: Four values, but far more than four quadrats. That is the trap.
steps.hint: Count the distinct numbers of daisies, not the quadrats.

steps.pre: Add the four frequencies. How many quadrats were surveyed altogether?
Multiply each daisy count by its frequency and add the results. How many daisies were counted in total?
steps.done: This is the new move: value × frequency, summed. It is the same as writing every quadrat out and adding them.
steps.hint: Work out 1×4, 2×6, 3×7 and 4×3, then add them together.

steps.pre: Divide the total number of daisies by the number of quadrats. What is the mean?
Which daisy count came up in the most quadrats? That is the mode.
steps.hint: Look for the largest frequency, then read the daisy count next to it.

steps.say: Check: the mean must lie between the smallest and largest counts, 1 and 4. It does, and it sits just below the modal value, which fits a data set with a few empty-ish quadrats.

silver.display: A student counted daisies in 20 quadrats: 1 daisy in 4 quadrats, 2 daisies in 6 quadrats, 3 daisies in 7 quadrats, 4 daisies in 3 quadrats. Calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat.

steps.say: Amy, Ben, Cara and Dan get a few pounds each. Eve has a very generous grandma.

steps.pre: Without doing any maths, what would you say a typical friend in this group gets each week, in pounds?
steps.done: Almost everyone picks that. You chose it because it sits in the middle of the group and because it comes up more than any other amount.
steps.hint: Look at the amount that keeps coming up, and ignore the odd one out for now.

steps.pre: Now add all five amounts together and divide by 5. What do you get, in pounds?
steps.done: Not one of the five friends gets anything close to that. Eve on her own has dragged it up.
steps.hint: Add 5 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 100, then share the total equally between the five friends.

steps.say: You have just used all four measures in this lesson. The amount you picked by instinct is both the median (the middle value once sorted) and the mode (the most common value). The number you calculated is the mean. Eve is an outlier, and outliers pull the mean but leave the median alone. The range, 100 − 4 = 96, measures how spread out the group is.

opener.display: Five friends compare what they get each week:

steps: Mean: add every value, then divide by how many values there are
Median: sort the values, then take the middle one
Mode: the value that appears most often
Range: largest minus smallest. IQR: Q3 − Q1
method_card.title: Mean, Median, Mode & Range
method_card.content:
Mean adds every value and divides by the count. It uses all the data, but one extreme value can drag it away from typical.

Median is the middle value once the data is sorted. With an even count, average the two middle values. Outliers barely move it, so it suits skewed data such as house prices.

Mode is the most common value or class. It is the only average that works for categories such as land use.

Range is largest minus smallest and shows total spread. The interquartile range (Q3 − Q1) covers the middle half, so it describes typical spread without the extremes.
method_card.example:
Question: A student recorded river widths (m) at 5 points: 2.3, 4.1, 3.5, 2.8, 3.3. Calculate the mean.

Step 1: Add: 2.3 + 4.1 + 3.5 + 2.8 + 3.3 = 16.0

Step 2: Divide by 5: 16.0 ÷ 5 = 3.2

Answer: Mean river width = 3.2m

steps: Decide which average is fair: extreme values pull the mean, so the median often describes a place better.
Quote an average and a measure of spread together, because two places can share a mean yet differ hugely.
Range covers everything including outliers. Interquartile range covers the middle half only.

steps.label: Check

steps.label: Answer

steps: Read the question to see which measure is wanted: mean, median, mode or range.
Mean: add every value, then divide by how many values there are.
Median: sort the values first, then take the middle one. Mode: the value that repeats most.
Range: largest value minus smallest value.

steps.label: Check
steps.content: 11 sits between the lowest count (9) and the highest (15), so it is believable. Only 9 repeats.

example.question: Beach litter counts on 5 days: 12, 9, 15, 9, 10. Find the mean and the mode.

steps: When values repeat, multiply each value by its frequency, add the products, then divide by the total frequency.
From a bar chart, read every bar off the vertical axis before calculating anything.
If one value sits far from the rest, the median describes the group better than the mean.
Interquartile range: sort, take Q1 (middle of the lower half) and Q3 (middle of the upper half), then subtract.

gold.hint: Order all 12 values. Q1 = median of lower 6, Q3 = median of upper 6.
gold.display: A student collected river width data (m) at 12 sites: 2.1, 3.4, 2.8, 5.2, 3.1, 2.5, 4.8, 3.6, 2.9, 3.3, 4.1, 3.0. Calculate the IQR.

guided_steps.pre: How many width measurements are there?
guided_steps.hint: Count the values listed.

guided_steps.pre: Sorted, what is the narrowest width, in metres?
guided_steps.hint: Scan the list for the smallest value.

guided_steps.pre: Split the sorted list down the middle. How many values are in each half?
guided_steps.hint: Share the twelve values evenly between two halves.

guided_steps.pre: Q1 is the middle of the lower six, so average the 3rd and 4th sorted values. What is Q1, in metres?
guided_steps.hint: The lower half runs 2.1, 2.5, 2.8, 2.9, 3.0, 3.1, so average its middle pair.

guided_steps.pre: Q3 is the middle of the upper six. What is Q3, in metres?
guided_steps.hint: The upper half runs 3.3, 3.4, 3.6, 4.1, 4.8, 5.2, so average its middle pair.

guided_steps.pre: Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the interquartile range, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Take the lower quartile away from the upper quartile.

guided_steps.pre: Check: how many of the twelve widths lie between Q1 and Q3?
guided_steps.done: Six of the twelve, the middle half, which is exactly what the interquartile range measures.
guided_steps.hint: Count the sorted values sitting between your two quartiles.

misconceptions.message: That is the full range. The interquartile range uses only the middle half of the sites.
That is the middle value, not a measure of how spread out the middle half is.
You have added the quartiles instead of subtracting one from the other.

gold.hint: Compare the two means first, then compare the two interquartile ranges.
gold.display: Two rivers were measured. River A: mean velocity 0.8 m/s, IQR 0.3 m/s. River B: mean velocity 1.2 m/s, IQR 0.9 m/s. Compare the rivers using both the average and the spread.
options: River B is faster on average but more variable, while River A is slower and more consistent, suggesting a more uniform channel
River A is faster and more consistent
River B is faster and more consistent

guided_steps.say: River A: mean 0.8 m/s, IQR 0.3 m/s. River B: mean 1.2 m/s, IQR 0.9 m/s.

guided_steps.pre: Locate the averages first. What is River B's mean velocity, in m/s?
guided_steps.hint: Read the mean quoted for River B, not its IQR.

guided_steps.pre: How much faster is River B's mean than River A's, in m/s?
guided_steps.hint: Subtract River A's mean from River B's mean.

guided_steps.pre: Now move to the spread. What is River B's interquartile range, in m/s?
guided_steps.hint: Read the IQR quoted for River B.

guided_steps.pre: How many times bigger is River B's interquartile range than River A's?
guided_steps.hint: Divide River B's IQR by River A's IQR.

guided_steps.say: River B is faster on average, but its velocities vary three times as much, so River A is the steadier river with the more uniform channel. That is the first option.

misconceptions.message: You have paired the higher mean with the smaller spread. Check which river has the larger interquartile range.
Read the two mean velocities again. The river with the higher mean is the faster one on average.
The two rivers differ on both figures given, so look at the numbers again before calling them alike.

gold.hint: Think about what single number a grouped table uses to stand in for every value in a class.
gold.display: A fieldwork team collected 20 temperature readings. The estimated mean from a grouped frequency table is 16.5°C, but the actual mean from raw data is 17.2°C. Why might these differ?
options: The estimated mean uses mid-points of class intervals, which may not match the actual distribution within each class
Grouped data always gives a higher mean

guided_steps.say: The team took 20 temperature readings. Grouped estimate: 16.5°C. Actual mean from raw data: 17.2°C.

guided_steps.pre: Locate the two figures. What is the estimated mean from the grouped table, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Read the figure that came from the grouped frequency table.

guided_steps.pre: What is the actual mean from the raw data, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Read the figure that came from the original readings.

guided_steps.pre: How much higher is the actual mean than the estimate, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the estimate from the actual mean.

guided_steps.pre: How many readings were taken altogether?
guided_steps.hint: Read the number of readings from the question.

guided_steps.say: A grouped table replaces every reading in a class with the class mid-point. If the real readings sit above those mid-points, the estimate comes out low, which is why it is 0.7°C under the true mean here. That is the first option.

misconceptions.message: A slip is always possible, but an estimate from grouped data is expected to differ. Think about what value the table uses for each class.
A grouped estimate can land either side of the true value, depending on where the readings sit inside each class.

gold.hint: Work out both averages, then judge which one the extreme reading has distorted.
gold.display: An environmental survey recorded CO₂ levels (ppm) at 10 sites near a factory: 380, 395, 410, 425, 1200, 390, 405, 415, 400, 385. Which average best represents typical conditions, and what is its value?
options: Median = 402.5, because the 1200 reading is an extreme outlier that would skew the mean
Mean = 480.5, because it includes all the data
Mode, because it ignores all outliers completely
Range = 820, because it shows the full spread

guided_steps.pre: Locate the data. How many sites were sampled?
guided_steps.hint: Count the readings listed.

guided_steps.pre: One reading sits far above the rest. What is it, in ppm?
guided_steps.hint: Look for the value that does not fit the pattern.

guided_steps.pre: Add all ten readings. What is the total, in ppm?
guided_steps.hint: Add the nine ordinary readings first, then add the extreme one.

guided_steps.pre: Divide by the number of sites to get the mean, in ppm.
guided_steps.hint: Share the total equally between the ten sites.

guided_steps.pre: Sorted, the middle pair sit in positions 5 and 6. Average them to get the median, in ppm.
guided_steps.hint: Sorted, the readings run 380, 385, 390, 395, then continue counting along.

guided_steps.say: Nine of the ten sites lie between 380 and 425 ppm. The mean is higher than every single one of them, while the median sits right among them, so the median describes typical conditions. That is the first option.

misconceptions.message: The mean uses every value including the extreme one, so it ends up higher than any ordinary site.
The range measures spread, not a typical value, so it cannot answer this question.
Every reading here is different, so this measure has nothing to pick out.

gold.hint: Compare the two means first, then ask what the difference in range says about distance from the sea.
gold.display: City A (coastal): mean = 12°C, range = 8°C. City B (inland): mean = 12°C, range = 22°C. Explain the geographical significance of these statistics.
options: Both have the same average but City B varies far more because of continentality, since the sea moderates City A's temperatures
City B is hotter because it has a larger range
The range is irrelevant, only the mean matters
City A must be further from the equator because its range is smaller

guided_steps.say: City A (coastal): mean 12°C, range 8°C. City B (inland): mean 12°C, range 22°C.

guided_steps.pre: Locate the averages first. What is City A's mean temperature, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Read the mean quoted for City A, not its range.

guided_steps.pre: What is the difference between the two mean temperatures, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Subtract one mean from the other.

guided_steps.pre: Now move to the spread. What is City B's range, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Read the range quoted for City B.

guided_steps.pre: How much larger is City B's range than City A's, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Subtract City A's range from City B's range.

guided_steps.say: Identical means but a range 14°C wider tells you the two climates behave very differently. The sea warms and cools slowly, so coastal City A has mild winters and cooler summers, while inland City B swings between extremes. That is the first option.

misconceptions.message: A larger range means a bigger gap between hottest and coldest, not a higher average temperature.
The two means are identical here, so the mean on its own cannot tell the cities apart.
Latitude is not the only control on temperature range. Think about how far each city is from the sea.

bronze.hint: Add every reading first, then divide by how many readings there are.
bronze.display: A student recorded daily temperatures (°C) for a week: 14, 16, 13, 17, 15, 14, 12. Calculate the mean temperature. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

guided_steps.say: Seven daily temperatures were recorded: 14, 16, 13, 17, 15, 14, 12.

guided_steps.pre: Get your bearings in the data first. How many temperature readings are listed?
guided_steps.done: The mean will divide by this count.
guided_steps.hint: Count the numbers in the list one by one.

guided_steps.pre: Add all the readings together. What is the total in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Add in pairs if it helps: 14 + 16, then 13 + 17, and so on.

guided_steps.pre: Divide the total by the number of readings. Give the mean to 1 decimal place.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your total by 7 and round to one decimal place.

guided_steps.pre: Check: the mean must sit between the coldest and hottest days. What was the coldest reading in °C?
guided_steps.done: Your mean lies between 12 and 17, so it is believable.
guided_steps.hint: Scan the list for the lowest number.

misconceptions.message: You have divided by the wrong number of readings. Count the days in the list again before you divide.
That is the middle reading once sorted, not the mean. The mean shares the total between every reading.
That is the gap between the hottest and coldest day, not an average.

bronze.hint: Order the data from smallest to largest first.
bronze.display: River depths (m) measured at 7 points across a channel: 0.3, 0.8, 1.2, 1.5, 1.1, 0.7, 0.4. Find the median depth.

guided_steps.say: Seven depths were measured across the channel: 0.3, 0.8, 1.2, 1.5, 1.1, 0.7, 0.4.

guided_steps.pre: Start with the shape of the data. How many depth readings are there?
guided_steps.done: An odd count means there is one true middle value.
guided_steps.hint: Count the values listed.

guided_steps.pre: Sort the depths in your head. What is the shallowest depth in metres?
guided_steps.hint: Look for the lowest number in the list.

guided_steps.pre: With seven sorted values, which position is the middle one? Give the position number.
guided_steps.hint: The middle of seven has three values below it and three above it.

guided_steps.pre: Count along your sorted list to that position. What depth is there, in metres?
guided_steps.hint: Your sorted list starts 0.3, 0.4, 0.7, so keep counting along.

guided_steps.pre: Check: how many of the depths are deeper than your median?
guided_steps.done: Three deeper and three shallower confirms you have the middle value.
guided_steps.hint: Count the values above it in your sorted list.

misconceptions.message: You have taken the middle of the list as it was written. The depths must be sorted before you pick the middle one.
That is the spread from shallowest to deepest, not the middle value.

bronze.hint: Tally how many times each land use appears, then pick the biggest tally.
bronze.display: A land use survey recorded: residential, residential, commercial, residential, parkland, commercial, residential, industrial, residential. What is the modal land use?

guided_steps.say: The survey listed: residential, residential, commercial, residential, parkland, commercial, residential, industrial, residential.

guided_steps.pre: Locate yourself in the data. How many survey entries are there altogether?
guided_steps.hint: Count every entry, including the repeats.

guided_steps.pre: How many entries say commercial?
guided_steps.hint: Read along the list and tally each time commercial appears.

guided_steps.pre: How many entries say residential?
guided_steps.hint: Read along the list again and tally residential.

guided_steps.pre: Parkland and industrial each appear how many times?
guided_steps.hint: Tally the two remaining categories.

guided_steps.say: Residential has the biggest tally, so the modal land use is residential.

misconceptions.message: You have chosen one of the least common categories. The mode is the one that appears most often.
Count the entries again, including every repeat. Another category appears more times than this one.

bronze.hint: Find the largest and smallest monthly totals, then subtract.
bronze.display: Rainfall data (mm) for 6 months: 45, 38, 52, 41, 60, 35. Calculate the range.

guided_steps.say: Six months of rainfall were recorded: 45, 38, 52, 41, 60, 35 mm.

guided_steps.pre: How many months of data are listed?
guided_steps.hint: Count the values in the list.

guided_steps.pre: Scan the whole list. What is the largest monthly rainfall in mm?
guided_steps.hint: Look for the highest number, wherever it sits in the list.

guided_steps.pre: Now find the smallest monthly rainfall in mm.
guided_steps.hint: Look for the lowest number, wherever it sits in the list.

guided_steps.pre: Subtract the smallest from the largest to get the range in mm.
guided_steps.hint: Take the smaller value away from the larger one.

guided_steps.pre: Check: how many of the six months fall outside your largest and smallest values?
guided_steps.done: Nothing lies outside, so the range really does cover all the data.
guided_steps.hint: Look for any month above the highest or below the lowest.

misconceptions.message: You have used the first and last values as written. Scan the whole list for the true largest and smallest.
You have added the two extremes. The range is a difference, so it needs a subtraction.

bronze.hint: Look for the count that comes up more often than any other.
bronze.display: Traffic counts at a junction: 120, 135, 128, 140, 135, 115, 135, 122. What is the mode?

guided_steps.say: Eight traffic counts were taken at the junction: 120, 135, 128, 140, 135, 115, 135, 122.

guided_steps.pre: How many counts were recorded?
guided_steps.hint: Count the values in the list.

guided_steps.pre: How many different values appear, counting each one only once?
guided_steps.hint: Ignore repeats: how many distinct numbers are there?

guided_steps.pre: Tally each distinct value. What is the biggest tally any single value reaches?
guided_steps.hint: Go through the list marking off each value, then look for the largest tally.

guided_steps.pre: Type the traffic count that reached that tally.
guided_steps.hint: Find which number you tallied more than once.

guided_steps.pre: Check: how many times does each of the other five values appear?
guided_steps.done: No other value repeats, so the mode is unique.
guided_steps.hint: Look at the values you did not pick.

misconceptions.message: That is the middle value once the counts are sorted, not the most frequent one.
You have given how many times it appeared rather than the traffic count itself.
That is the busiest count recorded, not the one that came up most often.

bronze.hint: Read every bar's height off the vertical axis, add them, then divide by the number of months.
bronze.display: The bar chart shows tourist arrivals (thousands) per month. Calculate the mean number of monthly tourists.

guided_steps.say: The bar chart shows tourist arrivals, in thousands, for each month of the year.

guided_steps.pre: Start on the chart. Count the bars along the bottom axis: how many months are shown?
guided_steps.done: This count is what you will divide by later.
guided_steps.hint: Every labelled month from Jan to Dec has its own bar.

guided_steps.pre: Find the tallest bar and read its height off the vertical axis, in thousands.
guided_steps.hint: Trace across from the top of the tallest bar to the scale on the left.

guided_steps.pre: Read every bar in turn and add the heights. What is the total, in thousands?
guided_steps.hint: Work along the chart from Jan to Dec, keeping a running total.

guided_steps.pre: Divide the total by the number of months to get the mean, in thousands.
guided_steps.hint: Share the total equally between the twelve months.

guided_steps.pre: Check: how many bars are taller than your mean?
guided_steps.done: Six bars above and six below is exactly what a sensible average looks like.
guided_steps.hint: Picture a horizontal line at your mean and count the bars poking above it.

misconceptions.message: You have divided by the wrong number of months. Count the bars along the bottom axis again.
That is the bar height that appears twice, not the mean of all the months.

bronze.hint: Find the reading that comes up more often than any other.
bronze.display: Soil pH readings at 8 sites: 5.2, 6.1, 5.8, 5.5, 6.3, 5.2, 5.9, 5.2. What is the mode?

guided_steps.say: Eight soil pH readings were taken: 5.2, 6.1, 5.8, 5.5, 6.3, 5.2, 5.9, 5.2.

guided_steps.pre: How many pH readings are listed?
guided_steps.hint: Count the values one by one.

guided_steps.pre: How many different pH values appear, counting each one only once?
guided_steps.hint: Ignore repeats: how many distinct readings are there?

guided_steps.pre: Tally each distinct reading. What is the largest number of times any single reading appears?
guided_steps.hint: Mark off each reading as you go, then look for the biggest tally.

guided_steps.pre: Type the pH reading that appears that many times.
guided_steps.hint: Find the reading you tallied more than once.

guided_steps.pre: Check: how many times does each of the other readings appear?
guided_steps.done: Every other reading occurs once, so the repeated one is the mode.
guided_steps.hint: Look at the readings you did not pick.

misconceptions.message: That is the middle reading once sorted, not the most frequent one.
You have given how many times it occurred rather than the pH value itself.
That is the spread of the readings, not the most common one.

bronze.hint: With an even number of values, find the mean of the two middle values.
bronze.display: Wind speed data (km/h): 15, 22, 18, 25, 20, 12. Find the median wind speed.

guided_steps.say: Six wind speeds were recorded: 15, 22, 18, 25, 20, 12 km/h.

guided_steps.pre: How many wind speed readings are there?
guided_steps.done: An even count means there is no single middle value.
guided_steps.hint: Count the values listed.

guided_steps.pre: Sort them. What is the lowest wind speed in km/h?
guided_steps.hint: Look for the smallest number in the list.

guided_steps.pre: The middle pair sit in positions 3 and 4 of your sorted list. What is the value in position 3, in km/h?
guided_steps.hint: Count along your sorted list to the third value.

guided_steps.pre: What is the value in position 4, in km/h?
guided_steps.hint: It is the next value up from the third one.

guided_steps.pre: Add the two middle speeds and divide by 2 to get the median in km/h.
guided_steps.hint: Add them together, then halve the total.

guided_steps.pre: Check: how many of the six speeds are below your median?
guided_steps.done: Three below and three above, which is exactly what a median does.
guided_steps.hint: Count the sorted values that sit underneath it.

misconceptions.message: You have used the middle of the list as it was written. Sort the speeds into order first.
With six values there is no single middle one, so you need both middle speeds.
That is the spread from calmest to windiest, not the middle value.

silver.hint: Multiply each size by its frequency, sum the products, then divide by total frequency.
silver.display: A student measured pebble sizes (cm) on a beach. The bar chart shows how many pebbles of each size were found. Calculate the mean pebble size, to the nearest whole centimetre.

guided_steps.say: The bar chart shows how many pebbles of each size the student found.

guided_steps.pre: Start on the chart. Read along the bottom axis: how many different pebble sizes are shown?
guided_steps.done: Five sizes, but far more than five pebbles. That is what makes this a frequency problem.
guided_steps.hint: Each labelled group along the bottom is one size.

guided_steps.pre: Read the height of the tallest bar off the vertical axis. How many pebbles were that size?
guided_steps.hint: Trace across from the top of the tallest bar to the frequency scale.

guided_steps.pre: Add all five bar heights. How many pebbles were measured altogether?
guided_steps.hint: Read each bar's frequency in turn and keep a running total.

guided_steps.pre: Multiply each size by its frequency and add the results. What is the total length of all the pebbles, in cm?
guided_steps.hint: Work out 2×5, 3×8, 4×12, 5×10 and 6×5, then add them.

guided_steps.pre: Divide that total by the number of pebbles, then round to the nearest whole centimetre.
guided_steps.hint: Share the total length equally between all the pebbles you counted, then round.

guided_steps.pre: Check: your mean must lie between the smallest and largest sizes on the chart. What is the largest size shown, in cm?
guided_steps.done: The mean sits inside the range of sizes on the chart, so it is believable.
guided_steps.hint: Read the label on the last group along the bottom axis.

misconceptions.message: You have divided by the number of bars rather than by the total number of pebbles counted.
That is how many pebbles were measured, not their mean size.

silver.hint: Sort the ten readings first, then average the two middle ones.
silver.display: Temperature readings (°C) at noon for 10 days: 18, 22, 15, 20, 45, 19, 21, 17, 20, 18. The median is more appropriate than the mean. What is the median?

guided_steps.say: Ten noon temperatures were recorded: 18, 22, 15, 20, 45, 19, 21, 17, 20, 18 °C.

guided_steps.pre: How many temperature readings are there?
guided_steps.hint: Count the values listed.

guided_steps.pre: One reading is far above all the others. What is it, in °C?
guided_steps.done: That outlier is exactly why the median is the safer average here.
guided_steps.hint: Look for the value that does not fit with the rest.

guided_steps.pre: Sort the readings. With ten values the middle pair sit in positions 5 and 6. What is the value in position 5, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Count along your sorted list to the fifth value.

guided_steps.pre: What is the value in position 6, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: It is the next value up in your sorted list.

guided_steps.pre: Add the two middle readings and divide by 2. What is the median, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Add them together, then halve the total.

guided_steps.pre: Check: how many readings sit below your median?
guided_steps.done: Five below and five above. Notice the 45°C outlier barely moved it.
guided_steps.hint: Count the sorted values underneath it.

misconceptions.message: You have used the middle of the list as it was written. Sort the readings before finding the middle.
That is the mean, and the extreme reading has dragged it upwards. The question asks for the middle value.
With ten values there is no single middle reading, so you need both of the middle pair.

silver.hint: Order the data. Q1 = median of lower half, Q3 = median of upper half. IQR = Q3 − Q1.
silver.display: River velocity data (m/s) at a downstream site: 0.8, 1.2, 0.9, 1.5, 1.1, 1.3, 0.7, 1.0. Calculate the interquartile range (IQR).

guided_steps.say: Eight velocities were recorded: 0.8, 1.2, 0.9, 1.5, 1.1, 1.3, 0.7, 1.0 m/s.

guided_steps.pre: How many velocity readings are there?
guided_steps.hint: Count the values listed.

guided_steps.pre: Sorted, what is the slowest velocity in m/s?
guided_steps.hint: Scan the list for the lowest value.

guided_steps.pre: Split the sorted list down the middle. How many readings are in each half?
guided_steps.hint: Share the eight values evenly between two halves.

guided_steps.pre: Q1 is the middle of the lower four, so average the 2nd and 3rd sorted values. What is Q1 in m/s?
guided_steps.hint: The lower half runs 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, so average its middle pair.

guided_steps.pre: Q3 is the middle of the upper four. What is Q3 in m/s?
guided_steps.hint: The upper half runs 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5, so average its middle pair.

guided_steps.pre: Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the interquartile range, in m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Take the lower quartile away from the upper quartile.

guided_steps.pre: Check: how many of the eight readings lie between Q1 and Q3?
guided_steps.done: Half the readings sit inside it, which is exactly what the interquartile range measures.
guided_steps.hint: Count the sorted values that sit between your two quartiles.

misconceptions.message: That is the full range. The interquartile range uses only the middle half of the data.
You have added the quartiles. The interquartile range is a difference between them.
That is the middle value, not a measure of how spread out the middle half is.

silver.hint: Compare the frequencies and pick the class with the biggest one.
silver.display: A grouped frequency table shows heights of vegetation: 0-10cm: 8, 10-20cm: 15, 20-30cm: 12, 30-40cm: 5. Which class interval is the modal class?

guided_steps.say: The table gives four height bands with their frequencies: 0-10cm: 8, 10-20cm: 15, 20-30cm: 12, 30-40cm: 5.

guided_steps.pre: Get oriented in the table. How many class intervals are listed?
guided_steps.hint: Count the height bands down the left of the table.

guided_steps.pre: Add the four frequencies. How many plants were measured altogether?
guided_steps.hint: Add 8, 15, 12 and 5.

guided_steps.pre: What is the highest frequency in the table?
guided_steps.hint: Compare all four frequencies and take the biggest.

guided_steps.pre: How many plants fall in the band immediately above the one with the highest frequency?
guided_steps.hint: Read the frequency next to the 20-30cm band.

guided_steps.say: The 10-20cm band holds more plants than any other, so the modal class is 10-20cm.

misconceptions.message: Another class has a higher frequency than this one. Compare all four frequencies again.
You have picked the tallest plants rather than the most common height band. The modal class is about frequency.

silver.hint: A smaller range means the values are packed more closely together.
silver.display: Two beaches were surveyed. Beach A pebble sizes: mean = 4.2cm, range = 8. Beach B: mean = 4.0cm, range = 3. Which beach has more consistent pebble sizes?
options: Cannot tell from mean and range alone

guided_steps.say: Beach A: mean 4.2cm, range 8. Beach B: mean 4.0cm, range 3.

guided_steps.pre: Locate the spread figures first. What is the range of pebble sizes on Beach A, in cm?
guided_steps.hint: Read the range quoted for Beach A, not the mean.

guided_steps.pre: What is the range on Beach B, in cm?
guided_steps.hint: Read the range quoted for Beach B.

guided_steps.pre: Subtract the smaller range from the larger. How much wider is one spread than the other, in cm?
guided_steps.hint: Take the smaller range away from the larger one.

guided_steps.pre: Which beach has the smaller range? Type 1 for Beach A or 2 for Beach B.
guided_steps.hint: The smaller of the two range figures wins.

guided_steps.say: The beach with the smaller range has pebbles that are far more similar in size, so Beach B is the more consistent one. The means are almost identical, so spread is what separates them.

misconceptions.message: You have read a large range as consistency. A big range means the values are spread far apart.
There is enough information here. The range on its own tells you how spread out the sizes are.

silver.hint: Add all twelve monthly totals, divide by twelve, then round.
silver.display: Monthly rainfall data (mm): 45, 38, 42, 55, 62, 48, 50, 44, 52, 40, 58, 46. Calculate the mean rainfall to the nearest whole number.

guided_steps.say: Twelve monthly rainfall totals were recorded: 45, 38, 42, 55, 62, 48, 50, 44, 52, 40, 58, 46 mm.

guided_steps.pre: How many monthly totals are listed?
guided_steps.hint: Count the values in the list.

guided_steps.pre: What is the largest monthly total, in mm?
guided_steps.hint: Scan the whole list for the highest number.

guided_steps.pre: Add all twelve totals. What is the sum, in mm?
guided_steps.hint: Add them in groups of four, then combine the group totals.

guided_steps.pre: Divide the sum by twelve and round to the nearest whole millimetre.
guided_steps.hint: Share the total equally between the twelve months, then round.

guided_steps.pre: Check: your mean must sit between the driest and wettest months. What is the smallest monthly total, in mm?
guided_steps.done: Your mean lies between 38 and 62, so it is believable.
guided_steps.hint: Scan the list for the lowest number.

misconceptions.message: You have divided by the wrong number of months. Count the values in the list again.
That is the middle value once sorted, not the mean.
That is the spread between the wettest and driest month, not an average.

silver.hint: Work out all three measures separately, then match them to an option.
silver.display: A geographer measures temperature at 6 sites: 12°C, 14°C, 11°C, 13°C, 14°C, 14°C. Calculate the mean, median and mode.

guided_steps.say: Six sites were measured: 12, 14, 11, 13, 14, 14 °C.

guided_steps.pre: How many sites were measured?
guided_steps.hint: Count the readings listed.

guided_steps.pre: Add the six temperatures. What is the total, in °C?
guided_steps.hint: Add them in pairs, then combine.

guided_steps.pre: Divide the total by the number of sites to get the mean, in °C.
guided_steps.hint: Share the total equally between the six sites.

guided_steps.pre: Sorted, the readings run 11, 12, 13, 14, 14, 14. Average the middle pair to get the median, in °C.
guided_steps.hint: The third and fourth sorted values are the middle pair.

guided_steps.pre: Which temperature appears three times? Type it, in °C.
guided_steps.hint: Tally each reading and find the one that repeats most.

guided_steps.say: A mean of 13, a median of 13.5 and a mode of 14 match the first option. Notice the three measures disagree because the readings are bunched at the top.

misconceptions.message: You have used the most common reading as the mean. The mean shares the total between all six sites.
The middle of the list as written is not the median, and the mode is not the lowest reading. Sort first, then tally.

problem_bank.gold_description: Judge and compare: choose the fairest average, work with quartiles, and say what the spread shows about a place.
problem_bank.bronze_description: One small set of values: work out the mean, median, mode or range that the question asks for.
problem_bank.silver_description: Bigger or repeated data: means from frequencies and bar charts, medians when an outlier is present, and the interquartile range.

worked_examples.question: Temperature data for a week: 12, 14, 11, 15, 13, 18, 14. Find the median and range.

steps.label: Compare
steps.content: The mean (63) is pulled up by the outlier (150). The median (49) better represents the typical count. Use median when outliers are present.

worked_examples.question: Traffic count data: 45, 52, 48, 150, 50, 47, 49. Why is the median a better average than the mean here?
